clue.text: Contracting agents sign at rents not quite in order.

definitions.text: Contracting agents

indicators.note: something not quite in order is jumbled, so these words' letters are to be rearranged

explanation.surface: A notice that rents are being signed in a slightly disorderly way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not quite in order' shuffles SIGN AT RENTS. 'Contracting' is the medical sense: an astringent makes tissues draw together.
explanation.definitionFit: Astringent substances cause body tissue to shrink or tighten, so they are agents of contraction.

clue.text: Just a single leg perhaps in the sportsman's fixture.

definitions.text: Just a single leg perhaps in the sportsman's fixture.

parts.words: Just a single leg perhaps in the sportsman's fixture
parts.note: the clue plays on a cricket fielding position named with a leg, and on a word meaning brief or lacking

explanation.surface: A sportsman's game involving only one leg of a tie.
explanation.walkthrough: Short leg is a cricket fielding position close to the batsman on the leg side; the word also means brief, as a single leg of a fixture would be.
explanation.definitionFit: The adjective describes something brief or curtailed, as a fixture of only one leg would be.

clue.text: Recovered, possibly, but unwilling or unable to resume.

definitions.text: Recovered, possibly
definitions.meaning: fitted with a new tyre, spelt the American way as tire, so a wheel freshly covered

definitions.text: unwilling or unable to resume
definitions.meaning: withdrawn from a career or a game, as a batsman who leaves the crease and does not return

explanation.surface: A patient who got better but cannot go back to work.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense splits the word as RE-TIRED: given a new tire (American spelling of tyre), i.e. re-covered.
explanation.definitionFit: A wheel given a fresh tyre has been re-covered, and someone who has stopped working for good will not take up their job again.

clue.text: "Kind hearts are more than coronets. And simple faith than blood." (Tennyson.)

definitions.text: "Kind hearts are more than coronets. And simple faith than blood." (Tennyson.)

parts.words: "Kind hearts are more than coronets. And simple faith than blood." (Tennyson.)
parts.note: a quotation from Tennyson's Lady Clara Vere de Vere with one word left out before blood: the solver supplies the missing adjective describing aristocratic ancestry

explanation.surface: A famous couplet from Tennyson about the worth of kindness over noble birth.
explanation.walkthrough: This is a fill-in-the-blank clue: the Tennyson line runs 'And simple faith than ___ blood', the missing word naming the conquerors of 1066 whose descendants formed England's old aristocracy.
explanation.definitionFit: Descent from the conquerors of 1066 was the mark of the oldest English nobility, the lineage the poem calls inferior to faith.

clue.text: One result of establishing inter- Continental relationships.

definitions.text: One result of establishing inter- Continental relationships.

parts.words: One result of establishing inter- Continental relationships
parts.note: a person of mixed parentage from two continents, the offspring of a cross-continental union

explanation.surface: A diplomatic outcome of forging ties between continents.
explanation.walkthrough: 'relationships' looks diplomatic, but means unions producing children of mixed heritage spanning two neighbouring continents.
explanation.definitionFit: A person with one parent from Europe and one from Asia is the child of a relationship spanning two continents.

clue.text: Odd items in the ornithologist's knapsack?

definitions.text: Odd items in the ornithologist's knapsack?

parts.words: Odd items in the ornithologist's knapsack
parts.note: small tasty morsels or snippets, reimagined as pieces of a small songbird carried by a birdwatcher

explanation.surface: A birdwatcher rummaging through miscellaneous objects in a rucksack.
explanation.walkthrough: The word for scraps of food or information splits as TIT BITS, as if pieces of the small bird an ornithologist studies.
explanation.definitionFit: Small dainty morsels or snippets of gossip are odds and ends, here pictured as bits of a small bird.

clue.text: Father could be almost ethical — with an addition to the sentence!

definitions.text: with an addition to the sentence

parts.note: a father is one example of a parent

indicators.note: the word is nearly itself, only slightly out of order, so its letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that a dad might nearly be moral, adding an aside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'almost' says the word is nearly right, its first two letters swapped to give HETICAL. 'Father could be' is a definition by example.
explanation.definitionFit: A parenthetical remark is an extra comment inserted into a sentence, often in brackets.

clue.text: They get a man's rag out, these do!

definitions.text: They get a man's rag out, these do!

indicators.note: something out is not in its proper place, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the word with its possessive S counted as a letter

explanation.surface: Some people irritate a fellow, provoking him.
explanation.walkthrough: 'get a man's rag out' sounds like annoying someone, but 'out' jumbles MAN'S RAG into NAGRAMS after A, and the result names the device itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Word puzzles of rearranged letters are exactly what turn this phrase into another word.

clue.text: Classical counterpart of the Mother Superior? "

definitions.text: Classical counterpart of the Mother Superior? "

parts.words: Classical counterpart of the Mother Superior
parts.note: the Latin title for the male head of a Roman household, set against the head of a convent

explanation.surface: Asking who in antiquity matched the head of a nunnery.
explanation.walkthrough: The answer is the Latin phrase 'father of the family', the head of a Roman household; Latin makes it classical and a father matches a mother.
explanation.definitionFit: In ancient Rome the male head of a household held authority over its members, a fatherly match for a convent's head.

clue.text: Situation affording better prospects in the main.

definitions.text: Situation affording better prospects in the main.

parts.words: Situation affording better prospects in the main
parts.note: the main is the open sea, and being high up in a ship's rigging gives a wider view

explanation.surface: A job position that generally offers better career chances.
explanation.walkthrough: 'prospects' and 'in the main' suggest career outlook in general; read literally, they mean views at sea, from up the mast.
explanation.definitionFit: Up high in the rigging a sailor can see farther across the ocean.

clue.text: Romantic realm of Anthony Hope.

definitions.text: Romantic realm of Anthony Hope.

parts.note: the fictional kingdom where Anthony Hope set The Prisoner of Zenda

explanation.surface: Describing a novelist's imaginary kingdom of adventure.
explanation.walkthrough: Anthony Hope's 1894 novel The Prisoner of Zenda is set in an invented Central European kingdom, whose name now means any storybook realm.
explanation.definitionFit: The fictional kingdom of Hope's swashbuckling romance gave its name to any imaginary land of court intrigue.

clue.text: They're evidently "not in," as it were.

definitions.text: They're evidently "not in," as it were.

parts.words: They're evidently "not in," as it were
parts.note: things that are outside or on the surface are, so to speak, not inside

explanation.surface: People who are clearly absent when someone calls.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not in' suggests someone away from home, but here describes outward features or appearances.
explanation.definitionFit: Outward aspects or surface features lie outside rather than within.

clue.text: A warm welcome in the Sporting League.

definitions.text: A warm welcome

indicators.note: the answer sits inside the run of letters of the two words that follow

explanation.surface: A friendly reception given at a sports league.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points inside SportING LEague. An ingle is a fireside, an old word for a warm hearth that welcomes visitors.
explanation.definitionFit: A fireside hearth gives a warm reception to anyone coming in from the cold.

clue.text: Was first in as well. What a blade!

definitions.text: What a blade!

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside another, as the clue says it goes in

parts.note: as well means too
to be first, at the front, is to have led

explanation.surface: Someone boasting they came first, and also admiring a fine sword.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' does the placing. The Spanish city was famous for its finely tempered swords, which took its name.
explanation.definitionFit: A sword forged in the Spanish city of that name was prized for its steel, so the city's name means a fine sword.

clue.text: Final stage in floating a shipping company. .

definitions.text: Final stage in floating a shipping company.

parts.words: Final stage in floating a shipping company
parts.note: when a ship's crew can no longer stay on the vessel, their last means of keeping afloat

explanation.surface: The last step in launching a shipping business on the stock market.
explanation.walkthrough: 'floating a company' suggests a stock-market launch; read literally, it is the crew of a ship staying afloat as a last resort.
explanation.definitionFit: An inflatable rescue boat is the last thing keeping a sinking ship's people on the water.

clue.text: A corpulent, dissolute, impudent, Elizabethan basketful.

definitions.text: A corpulent, dissolute, impudent, Elizabethan basketful.

parts.words: A corpulent, dissolute, impudent, Elizabethan basketful
parts.note: Shakespeare's fat knight, hidden in a laundry basket in The Merry Wives of Windsor

explanation.surface: Describing a fat, rakish, cheeky Elizabethan stuffed into a basket.
explanation.walkthrough: In The Merry Wives of Windsor the fat knight hides in a basket of dirty linen and is tipped into the Thames.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's knight is the stout, carousing rogue who ends up carried off in a laundry basket.

clue.text: Properly controlled it puts an end to the game.

definitions.text: Properly controlled it puts an end to the game.

parts.words: Properly controlled it puts an end to the game
parts.note: game here is wild birds or animals hunted, which pellets fired from a shotgun kill

explanation.surface: Something well managed that ends a match.
explanation.walkthrough: 'the game' looks like a sporting contest, but means hunted birds, killed by the pellets of a shotgun cartridge when well aimed.
explanation.definitionFit: Small metal pellets fired from a shotgun bring down wildfowl and other quarry.

clue.text: Apply pressure in the Final? It's effective, anyway.

definitions.text: effective

indicators.note: one piece is to be placed inside the other, as the clue says

parts.note: the final part is the end
to apply pressure is to force

explanation.surface: A coach urges pushing hard in the cup final, saying it works.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' does the placing; 'It's ... anyway' frames the definition loosely: a law enforced is put into effect.
explanation.definitionFit: A rule that is imposed and carried out is in operation, put into effect.

clue.text: A bit of a break where lasting ill-will is concerned.

definitions.text: A bit of a break

parts.note: where something is concerned means regarding it, which is the short word re
spite is lasting malice

explanation.surface: Taking a short break from a long-running feud.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'where X is concerned' means regarding X, which crosswords render by the short Latin-derived word for about.
explanation.definitionFit: A short pause or interval of relief is a little break.

clue.text: So supple, and with the possibility of getting so slim.

definitions.text: supple

indicators.note: the words could become the answer if their letters were rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone flexible who might also become thin.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with the possibility of getting' rearranges SO SLIM.
explanation.definitionFit: A lithe, graceful body is flexible and bends easily.

clue.text: Prevailed upon a former dictator in little India.

definitions.text: Prevailed upon

indicators.note: one piece goes inside the other, as stated

parts.note: IND is a short form of India
Il Duce was the title of Mussolini, Italy's former dictator

explanation.surface: Someone persuaded by an old tyrant while in a small Indian community.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' does the placing. Il Duce (the leader) was Mussolini's title; IND is a standard abbreviation for India.
explanation.definitionFit: To persuade someone to act is to win them over, as by inducement.

clue.text: The bay of the hounds?

definitions.text: The bay of the hounds?

parts.note: the baying of hunting dogs, recast as a body of water named after a man whose name suggests a hound's son

explanation.surface: The howling noise made by a pack of hunting dogs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bay' looks like a dog's howl, but is the great Canadian inlet named after the explorer Henry; his name can be read as a dog's offspring.
explanation.definitionFit: The vast Canadian bay takes its name from the English navigator Henry, explorer of the region.

clue.text: Name part in Cader's rapid rise to fame and fortune.

definitions.text: Name part

indicators.note: the answer lies inside the letters of the words that follow

explanation.surface: A figure named Cader rising quickly to wealth and fame.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points into rapID RISe. Cader Idris is a Welsh mountain, so the hidden word is the other part of Cader's name.
explanation.definitionFit: The mountain's full Welsh name has two parts, and this is the second one after Cader.

clue.text: A priestly sort of circle, if ever there was one!

definitions.text: A priestly sort of circle, if ever there was one!

parts.words: A priestly sort of circle, if ever there was one
parts.note: stone circles such as Stonehenge are popularly linked to the ancient Celtic priests

explanation.surface: Describing a clique of clergymen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'circle' sounds like a social set of priests, but means a ring of standing stones linked in popular belief to the ancient Celtic priesthood.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancient stone rings are popularly attributed to the Celtic priests of pre-Roman Britain.

clue.text: A handsome chap, he was, by the sound of it.

definitions.text: A handsome chap, he was, by the sound of it.

parts.words: A handsome chap, he was, by the sound of it
parts.note: handsome said aloud matches the hansom, a horse-drawn carriage, so its driver is a hansom chap

explanation.surface: Gossip that a certain man was good-looking, from what one hears.
explanation.walkthrough: A hansom was a two-wheeled horse-drawn cab of Victorian London; its driver, sounding like a 'handsome chap', is the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: The driver of a hired horse-drawn hansom, or any taxi, is a cab driver.

clue.text: A resounding title as all-embracing naturally strikes terror.

definitions.text: strikes terror

parts.note: ff is fortissimo, the musical mark for very loud
a title is a right, and making it all-embracing gives all rights, the plural

explanation.surface: An imposing, sweeping title that naturally terrifies people.
explanation.walkthrough: FF is the musical notation for fortissimo. 'naturally' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: To frighten someone badly is to fill them with fear, an old literary verb.

clue.text: Not at all a pen artist, but deadly nevertheless.

definitions.text: deadly
definitions.note: the adjective stands for a deadly creature, a noun

parts.note: a pen is a female swan; the male is a cob, the very opposite
RA is a Royal Academician, an artist

explanation.surface: Someone who is no writer but dangerous all the same.
explanation.walkthrough: 'pen' looks like a writing tool, but it is a female swan; its opposite, the male, is a cob.
explanation.definitionFit: The hooded snake's venom can kill, making it one of the most lethal reptiles.

clue.text: Legal interval during which waistcoats are permissible?

definitions.text: Legal interval during which waistcoats are permissible?

parts.words: Legal interval during which waistcoats are permissible
parts.note: the legal transfer of ownership of property, playfully read as a season of wearing vests

explanation.surface: A period when the law lets you wear a waistcoat.
explanation.walkthrough: Vesting is the legal transfer of property rights; read literally, 'vest' is a waistcoat, so days for wearing one.
explanation.definitionFit: Dates on which property rights pass legally to a new owner are fixed points in law.
